Welcome to Day 1 of Health Insurance Subrogation training. Over the next sessions we will look at how health insurance fits into an injury case and why it matters to us on the settlement team. When a health plan pays our client's medical bills, it usually wants to be paid back from the settlement. Today lays the groundwork: the overview and workflow, the fundamentals, initiating subrogation, and HIPAA and the letter of representation.

Here is our roadmap for today. We start with an overview of the case workflow, then the fundamentals of subrogation, then HIPAA and the letter of representation, and finally how we initiate subrogation on a file. Each part builds on the one before it. By the end you should be able to explain to a colleague why health insurance payments become a lien that must be resolved before a client is paid.

Before we go further, let's agree on the shorthand you will see in case notes and emails. HI is health insurance, subro is subrogation, LOR is the letter of representation, and HIPAA is the federal privacy law. PHI is protected health information, PIP is personal injury protection, and CMS runs Medicare and Medicaid. Keep this list handy during your first weeks. If you see an abbreviation you don't recognize on a file, ask rather than guess.

These are sample health insurance cards. When a client gives us their health insurance, this card is where we find what we need: the plan name, the member ID, the group number, and the phone numbers on the back. Ask clients for a clear copy of the front and back. The member ID and group number are what the subrogation department and the providers will ask for, so make sure both are readable on the file.

We start with the definition, because everything else builds on it. Subrogation is the health insurer asking to be paid back by the responsible party, or that party's insurance, for medical bills it paid for our client. The key words are legally accountable: someone else caused the injury, so the plan wants its money back out of the recovery. For a Closing Specialist, every health insurance payment on an injury case is a potential lien to resolve before the client is paid.

This slide states the basis of the right. When a health insurer pays for treatment caused by someone else, it has a right to recover those costs from the at-fault party. In practice, that right usually reaches us as a claim against the settlement. A common mistake is assuming that because the client paid premiums, the plan has no claim. The premiums bought coverage, not a free pass on reimbursement. So where does the plan expect to be repaid from? The injury recovery.

Keep this in perspective. What the health plan pays is usually a discounted, contracted amount, not the full amount the hospital billed. So the amount the plan asks back is often much smaller than the gross bills on the file. That is good news for the client, and it is why we want bills run through health insurance. When you explain this to a client, frame it as a benefit: having coverage usually shrinks what has to be paid back.

This is the life of a case at a glance. It starts at intake, then the letter of representation goes out and the third-party or first-party claim is opened. The client treats, and the health insurance subrogation claim is set up. Property damage is handled, liability is finalized, records and bills are gathered, and finally any lien is addressed. Notice that setting up the health insurance subrogation claim happens early, not at the end of the case.

How do we spot a subrogation opportunity? Look at four things on every file: whether EMS or an ambulance was involved, which hospital the client went to, what treatments and procedures were done, and what health insurance the client has. Each one tells you where bills were generated and who may have paid them. An ambulance ride and an emergency room visit almost always produce bills that a health plan may pay and later claim back.

Here is a simple but important definition. The health insurance subrogation lien is the list of all the payments the health insurance made. In other words, it is the itemized record of what the plan paid that it wants back from the recovery. When you receive one, you will compare it against the client's treatment to make sure every line relates to the accident. We will practice reviewing lien ledgers in later sessions.

This example shows why one visit can mean several bills. A client who took an ambulance and saw an emergency room physician who ordered X-rays would typically get four separate bills: ambulance, hospital, emergency room physician, and radiology. Each comes from a different provider, and each may be billed to health insurance separately. When you track bills on a file, don't stop at the hospital. Ask who else was involved in that visit.

This is the trigger for opening subrogation. We initiate it only when two things are true: the client was seen at a hospital or related facility, and the client has used their health insurance. If there was no hospital visit, or health insurance was not used, there is generally nothing for the plan to claim back. Before you open a claim, check both conditions on the file and note what you found.

This slide is about timing. From the date of loss, medical providers often have a limited window, typically thirty to ninety days, to submit a claim to the health insurance. Some allow more than ninety days depending on the client's plan. Why does this matter to us? If the bill is not submitted in time, the client could be left holding the full charge. Getting insurance information to providers early protects the client.

What if the client has no health insurance? First, check with the client whether they can apply for emergency Medicaid. If that is not possible, check with the case manager whether the bill can be placed under attorney liens. In that case, a reduction may be requested at the time of settlement. Either way, don't leave an uninsured hospital bill unaddressed on the file; decide on a path early and document it.

A short reminder that ties back to the filing window. Medical bills should go to the health insurance as soon as possible. If they are submitted late, the plan can deny them for timely filing, and the client may be left with the full balance. So when you learn about a new provider or a new bill, make sure the provider has the health insurance details right away rather than waiting.

Here is the key objective of this phase. We want every hospital bill submitted to health insurance, rather than leaving the client to carry the full medical expense. That ties back to the discounted rate we discussed. If a hospital sends the client a full balance statement, that may be a sign the bill never went to insurance. Follow up, give the provider the insurance details, and confirm it was submitted.

Now we turn to minimizing risks for the client. One common risk is clients receiving medical bills directly. This usually happens because the hospital or a related provider doesn't know which health insurance to bill. When a client calls worried about a bill in the mail, this is one of the first things to check: does the provider actually have the client's health insurance information on file?

Set expectations with clients early. Let them know that we do not have relationships with all medical providers. Also explain that medical providers are not obligated to treat patients on a lien or to wait for payment until the case is resolved. Clients sometimes assume every provider will simply hold the bill until settlement. Being clear about this up front helps avoid surprises and frustration later in the case.

This is the practical step that prevents many problems. Prompt clients to share their health insurance information with their medical providers without delay. When providers have the insurance details, bills get processed on time and complications are avoided. A simple reminder during your early calls with the client can save weeks of follow-up later. Note in the file that you gave the reminder.

Health insurance is not the only source of payment. In some cases the client may not need to pay anything to the hospital, because their Medical Payments coverage or Personal Injury Protection from their own auto insurance covered the expenses. So when you review a hospital balance, check whether MedPay or PIP already paid it before assuming the client owes money or that health insurance was billed.

Clients often worry that medical bills will hurt their credit. Here are tips we can share. First, paying the bill promptly helps keep it from going to collections. Second, entering into a payment plan also keeps the bill out of collections, and the client may still be able to negotiate a lower settlement on it later. Present these as options for the client to consider, not as instructions.

Another tip is checking Medicaid eligibility. If the client has no health insurance, they can apply for Medicaid. For Nevada clients, that is through Access Nevada; for Washington clients, through the WA Health Plan Finder. Other locations may have their own resources. If the client turns out to be eligible for Medicaid or Medicare, they can have the provider submit the bill to that program instead of paying it themselves.

Two more options for clients. They can try to reduce a bill by negotiating directly with the medical provider. Or they can wait until the case concludes and pay the bill from the settlement proceeds, which can help improve their credit. This second option connects directly to our work at closing, because those bills will show up when we prepare the disbursement.

Here is the exception to the rule we saw earlier. Normally we open subrogation only when the client went to a hospital and used health insurance. Medicare clients are different: subrogation should be initiated as soon as the case is set up, whether or not they treated under Medicare. Don't wait to see if Medicare paid anything. So when do we open Medicare subrogation? At case setup, every time.

Now some critical details in the workflow. When you notify the plan, the LOR should go to the subrogation department together with a signed HIPAA form. The LOR tells them we represent the client, and the HIPAA form allows them to share the client's health information with us. A common mistake is sending the LOR alone and then waiting weeks, only to find the request was not processed.

Sending is not the same as receiving. Make sure the subrogation department actually received your letter of representation. Call or check, confirm they have it, and note who confirmed and when. Letters get misrouted and faxes fail. If you don't confirm, you may find out months later that no file was opened, and then you are scrambling at settlement. Make confirmation a routine step.

Be patient with the timing. Medical provider bills may take up to thirty days to be paid by the health insurance and then show up on the subrogation lien. So if you request a lien shortly after treatment and a bill is missing, it may simply not have been processed yet. Plan your follow-ups with this delay in mind, especially before you treat any lien amount as final.

Help the subrogation analyst help you. Give them information about the client's injuries, treatment, and the facilities involved. That lets them identify which medical care relates to the accident when they process the subrogation lien. The better the information you give, the more accurate the lien is likely to be, and the less time you will spend later disputing charges that are not accident-related.

This is a critical detail. Refrain from sharing the defendant's auto insurance details with the health insurer. If you do, the plan may notify the defendant's carrier about the health insurance, which can lead to a lien on the file. If the subrogation department says it needs the auto insurance details, that becomes a decision to make deliberately, not something you volunteer. When unsure, escalate to your supervisor or attorney.

This is a sample letter of representation sent to a provider. Look at the parts: the date and how it was sent, the provider's billing and records department, the RE block with the client's details and date of loss, and the body stating that the office represents the patient. It then lists what is requested, such as medical records and an itemized statement, and closes with the attorney's signature.

Let's define the letter of representation. An LOR is a formal document from the lawyer or law firm stating that we represent the client. In health subrogation it does two jobs: it establishes the attorney-client relationship, and it directs all communications to the attorney. That matters because we want lien notices, ledgers and final amounts coming to us, so nothing is missed. Who should the plan contact once our LOR is on file? Us.

Here is a sample medical representation letter sent to a provider by fax. It advises that the firm represents the client, asks the provider to place the firm's name on the chart, and asks for the exact amount of medical bills and any balance owing. It also requests a copy of the records, notes that a HIPAA authorization is enclosed, and asks to be told if copying costs exceed a set amount.

So what is a medical representation letter for? It authorizes an individual or entity, like our law firm, to represent a client in matters about their medical treatment, billing, or claims. The sample we just saw is a template that can be adapted for that purpose. When you use a template, always check that the client's name, dates and provider details are correct for your file before it goes out.

This is a sample HIPAA authorization form. Notice the sections: who is authorized to disclose and to whom, what information will be disclosed, what will not be disclosed, the purpose, how long the authorization is valid, and the patient's acknowledgement and signature. This signed form is what goes with the LOR to the subrogation department, so check that it is signed and dated before you send it.

Now to HIPAA itself. Everyone on the team needs to understand HIPAA as it relates to health insurance subrogation. We handle protected health information every day: records, bills, lien ledgers. We must handle it securely and follow the privacy rules throughout the subrogation process. Think about where PHI sits in your daily work, in emails, attachments and printouts, and how you keep it secure.

HIPAA accountability means taking responsibility for complying with the law to safeguard patients' protected health information. In practice, that means handling health information lawfully and securely every time. This is not just a policy point: violations can lead to significant legal penalties and fines. Treat every record and ledger on a file as something that must be protected.

Covered entities and business associates may only use or disclose PHI for permissible purposes. Those include treatment, payment, healthcare operations, or when the individual authorizes it. That last one is why the signed HIPAA form matters so much to us: it is the client's authorization that lets the plan and providers share information with the firm.

Patients have rights under HIPAA. They can access their health information, request corrections, and find out how their PHI has been used. Covered entities must have procedures to make sure those rights are respected. This is useful to remember when a client asks why they can request their own records, or when a record looks wrong and needs correcting.

What happens if PHI is exposed? In a breach involving unsecured PHI, covered entities and business associates must notify the affected individuals, the Department of Health and Human Services, and sometimes the media, depending on how large the breach is. A misdirected email with records attached is the kind of thing that can start this process, so double-check recipients before sending.

Here are the stakes. HIPAA penalties come in two kinds. Civil penalties run from one hundred to fifty thousand dollars per violation, up to one point five million dollars a year for identical violations. Criminal penalties apply to severe violations, ranging from fifty thousand dollars and one year in prison up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars and ten years where there is personal gain or malicious intent.

Compliance is about protecting people's medical records and other health information. When we comply, the client's information stays protected. When we don't, the result can be significant fines and penalties. Keep this in mind as we go through the specific HIPAA rules on the next few slides: privacy, security, breach notification and enforcement.

The first rule is the Privacy Rule. It sets the standards for protecting medical records and other PHI. It applies to healthcare providers, health plans and clearinghouses, which are called covered entities, and also to their business associates who handle PHI. The health plans and providers we deal with on every file are covered entities under this rule.

The Security Rule covers electronic PHI, called ePHI. It sets standards for safeguarding it so it stays confidential, accurate, and available when needed. Most of what we handle is electronic: portal downloads, emailed ledgers, scanned records. So this rule touches our daily work, from how we store files to how we send them.

The Breach Notification Rule is the one we touched on earlier. If unsecured PHI is breached, covered entities and business associates must notify the individuals affected, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and sometimes the media. If you ever think PHI was sent to the wrong place, raise it with your supervisor straight away rather than waiting.

The Enforcement Rule covers what happens after a violation. It governs how HIPAA violations are investigated and penalized by the HHS Office for Civil Rights, known as OCR. This is the rule behind the civil and criminal penalties we saw a few slides ago. Put simply, HIPAA has an enforcer, and violations are investigated.

To wrap up HIPAA: compliance keeps patients' protected health information confidential. That includes medical records, billing details, and other identifying information, exactly the documents we handle on every settled case. Without these safeguards, sensitive data could reach unauthorized people and violate the client's privacy rights. Treat every file as if the client were watching how you handle it.

That brings us to the end of Day 1. We covered the case workflow, the fundamentals of subrogation, how to initiate subrogation, the critical details in the workflow, and HIPAA and letters of representation. Before the next session, review the jargon list and the critical details. Bring any questions from your own files, and we will build on today's foundation.
